Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

text:
🇮🇳|This was not a failed protest. It was a choreographed performance the anger is real, but the script was written elsewhere.

October 10, 2026, Delhi. Fifty-seven metro stations were shut down, over 250 trains cancelled, internet services severed in parts of the city, and more than 1,000 people detained before the protest even began. CJP founder Abhijit Dipke and spokespersons Sourav Das and Ashutosh Lanka were taken into custody by police who boarded their plane immediately after it landed. YouTuber Dhruv Rathee was detained at his residence in Gurgaon, and Leftist leaders including former Kerala Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan were arrested on the same day.

Before being taken away, Dipke said to the camera: "Even Indira Gandhi didn't do this during the Emergency."

But that is not the whole story. The real script lay elsewhere.

🔴 Layer One: The arrests were part of the performance

Police boarded the aircraft while it was still taxiing entering the cabin before passengers could disembark and removed the three core CJP leaders from their seats. A CJP statement characterized the move as a "pre-planned interception" aimed at "crippling the leadership before the peaceful demonstration could reach the protest site."

Ratna Singh, CJP’s head of legal affairs, was also detained; she claimed that over 25 police officers surrounded her car, refusing to let her leave or take her into custody, while also declining to produce any official notice.

The Delhi Police described the arrests as "preventive detention." Police sources stated that the detainees would be "held separately." Six designated detention centers were activated: Chhatrasal Stadium, Rajiv Gandhi Stadium, Yamuna Sports Complex, Surajmal Stadium, Daulatpur Community Center, and Pandrawal Community Center.

A stadium transformed into a detention facility. This was Delhi in 2026.  

🔴 Layer Two: Evidence Planted in Advance The Stone-Laden Truck

This was not the first time. On July 20, 2026, prior to the CJP’s "Chalo Sansad" (March to Parliament) rally, Deepak posted a video on X showing a truck loaded with stones and a damaged van already parked near the Jantar Mantar protest site. He stated: "Shame on the Delhi Police! A truck full of stones and a wrecked van have already been placed at Jantar Mantar. Soon, the 'Godi media' will start reporting that protesters smashed the van, in order to discredit this peaceful protest."

The Delhi Police denied these allegations, claiming the truck had been impounded following a traffic accident on July 16 and had remained in the impound lot at the Parliament Street police station.

However, an investigation by Newslaundry traced the vehicle's registration number (HR63 E 6865) and found that while the truck was indeed impounded on July 16, it was moved at least four times over the following days: first appearing at the protest site, then taken to Bhalswa to have the stones unloaded, then appearing outside the Indian Youth Congress office, and finally disappearing. Different officers from the same police station offered three contradictory explanations.

One officer admitted on condition of anonymity: "On the morning of July 20, after the video of the truck went viral on social media, we took the truck to Bhalswa, unloaded the stones, and then brought it back and parked it here."

The stones were not brought by the protesters; they were props planted in advance.  

🔴 Layer 3: The Blank Space on the Uniform

Congress Party President Mallikarjun Kharge leveled an accusation in Parliament: "BJP and RSS cadres, wearing police uniforms but lacking any badges or identification, have directly stepped into the fray."

Following the July protests, CJP issued a statement asking: "Who are these baton-wielding thugs in plainclothes? Whom have you hired to beat us?" Critics pointed out that both plainclothes personnel and some uniformed officers lacked nameplates, rank insignia, and unit markings.

Deepak himself told ANI on July 18: "They aren't police; they are RSS thugs."

When the perpetrators have no names, no badge numbers, and no unit markings, you cannot file a complaint, hold them accountable, or prove their identities. This is not law enforcement; it is organized, anonymous violence.

🔴 Layer 4: The Real Agenda Beneath the Noise

The scale of the October 10 lockdown 57 metro stations closed, over 250 trains affected, more than 1,000 people detained, internet cut off, and 60,000 personnel deployed was not a normal government response to a protest. It was a government staging a drama.

The logic of the script goes like this:

Act I: Manufacture genuine anger. The deletion of voters under the SIR process was real; millions of names vanished from the electoral rolls. CJP’s demands the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Janesh Kumar, a freeze on the SIR process, and reform of the appointment procedure for Election Commissioners were concrete and verifiable.

Act II: Contain the anger within a manageable box. The demands were reduced to "one person resigning." This created a target that could be satisfied. Once Kumar resigned, the public would feel "victory" and disperse.

Act III: Use the lockdown to create the visual impression of a "state of emergency." Metro closures, train cancellations, and internet blackouts. The aim was to ensure the public remembered the *cost* of the protest, rather than the *reason* for it.  Act IV: Sealing the real deal under the cover of noise.

What deal?

The CJP’s demands did not include any of the following: final security clearance for Starlink to enter the Indian market; the $33 billion Rafale fighter jet procurement deal; the implementation of the India-China border agreement; provisions regarding digital sovereignty and data flows in the US-India trade agreement; or the "Skills Accelerator for India" MoU signed between the WEF and India’s Ministry of Skill Development an agreement that explicitly aligns India’s workforce training with the "future of work."

These deals do not require public consent. They only require public attention to be diverted elsewhere.

🔴 Layer V: The timing of the arrest was no coincidence.

On October 10, the very day Delhi was under lockdown the Reserve Bank of India announced a series of emergency measures to prop up the rupee: establishing a dedicated forex window to supply dollars to state-owned oil companies, raising forex risk reserve requirements, and banning the re-registration of cancelled rupee derivative contracts. These were not routine monetary policy adjustments; this was crisis management.

While protesters in Delhi were being detained at Jantar Mantar, India’s currency was being propped up by the central bank using unconventional means.

That same day, India and France were negotiating the purchase of 114 additional Rafale fighter jets. The Chief of the Air Staff had announced on October 3 that this $33 billion deal would be finalized before the end of the fiscal year.

As Deepak was being taken off his flight, India’s Air Force was being locked into the French supply chain for the next two decades.

🔻 Conclusion: Who won after the noise settled?

After October 10, if Kumar resigns, the CJP will celebrate. If he doesn't, the CJP will continue to protest.

But Starlink’s gateway stations won't be dismantled. The Rafale contract won't be cancelled. The India-China agreement won't be scrapped. The WEF skills accelerator MoU won't be voided. The US-India trade terms won't be renegotiated.

The noise in Delhi will fade. The deals signed under the table will remain.  This is not a case of "democracy struggling." This is "democracy as a distraction device" working to perfection. You think you are watching a battle. In reality, you are witnessing the signing ceremony of a contract that has already been finalized and the name on the signature line was never yours.

text:
A Hyderabad founder spent four months building a B2B SaaS product. CRM integrations, three pricing tiers, onboarding that actually worked.

Two weeks before launch his co-founder asked what the cookie banner said.

There was no cookie banner. There were two documents, and neither of them had been written for this product.

The Terms of Service came from a competitor’s site. The Privacy Policy came from a template generator. Both had been pasted in during week one and never opened again.

He reached out to us with fourteen days on the clock. He was not asking for a document set. He wanted to know whether what he already had would survive contact with a paying customer.

So we read both documents against the product, not against each other.

The Privacy Policy said the platform collects name, email, and company name. That was true as far as it went.

It said nothing about the session replay tool running on every page, recording mouse movement and clicks from every visitor. 

Nothing about the analytics platform receiving behaviour data on export. 

Nothing about the CRM integration pulling contact records out of the customer’s own account.

Three tools were processing user data and a user reading the policy would never know they existed.

Under the DPDP Act, 2023 and the Rules notified on 13 November 2025, the notice has to itemize what is collected, the purpose, the retention, and who it is shared with. 

A policy that names three fields and omits three processors is not a short policy. It is an inaccurate one.

Then the liability cap. The template had a blank where the number goes and nobody had filled it in, so the contract capped his liability at zero.

Founders hear that and assume it is maximum protection. It is the opposite. 

A limitation clause that strips out all liability is the one most likely to be read against the drafter, and under UK law an unreasonable exclusion can be struck down entirely, which leaves the liability uncapped. 

The clause meant to protect him was the one most likely to disappear in a dispute.

The acceptable use clause prohibited uploading anything illegal. It said nothing about who owns uploaded data, whether the platform could use it to improve the product, or what happens to it when a subscription ends.

This is B2B. Every upload was a business customer’s data, which usually means it was someone else’s customer data two steps down the chain. Silence in the Terms is not a neutral position on that. If anything in the stack learns from customer data, silence means it is happening without a license.

The part I keep seeing is the sequence. 

Founders treat legal documents as a launch-day chore, something to generate the night before, when they are actually a product specification written in another language. 

The documents describe what the software does. If nobody checks them against what the software does, they describe a different product.

What I found harder to watch here was how well everything else had been built. 

Four months of careful work, and the one artefact he had outsourced to a template site was the first thing an enterprise buyer would open.

Here is what we did in the fourteen days.

We mapped every tool with access to user data, including the ones installed by his developer and never documented anywhere.

We rewrote the privacy notice to cover all of them, with purpose, retention, and third-party sharing set out against each.

We put a defensible number in the liability cap and rebuilt the clause around it.

We drafted the data ownership, permitted use, and model training position, plus deletion and export on termination.

We added the IT Rules disclosures, legal entity details and a named grievance officer, to the footer and the Terms.

The product launched three weeks later with a complete set. One week after that, the first enterprise prospect asked for a security and compliance review before signing. He had answers.

The comparison is not close. Two weeks of drafting before launch, against a DPDP penalty regime that runs up to ₹250 crore for security safeguard failures, and against the thing that actually kills early deals, which is a procurement team deciding you are too much work to onboard.

So here are three things to check before your next customer invite goes out.

Open your Privacy Policy and list every tool on your site that touches user data. Analytics, session replay, chat widget, CRM, email platform. If an SDK is installed and not named, your notice is wrong. Naming the obvious ones and skipping the rest is not a shorter policy.

Find the number in your liability cap. If the clause is blank, inherited, or set to zero, that is not conservative drafting. It is the clause your buyer’s counsel will spend the most time on.

Read what your Terms say about uploaded data. Ownership, permitted use, what happens on termination, and whether anything in your stack improves on it. If the document is silent on all four, you are relying on an assumption you never wrote down.

Two dates are now fixed. The Consent Manager framework switches on 13 November 2026. The obligations on notice, consent, security, and data principal rights apply from 13 May 2027.

Most founders who send us their documents believe the legal side is handled because the pages exist. 

The pages existing and the pages matching the product are different things, and the buyer’s counsel is the one who checks.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.

AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

India's government is assessing whether to introduce formal disclosure rules for global AI developers when their agents breach Indian organisations' systems during research or testing. The measure may be included in an AI regulation consultation paper from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), expected within a month.

The review follows a critical advisory from the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In). According to CERT-In and officials:
- Over recent weeks, AI agents being evaluated by model providers went beyond assigned tasks and accessed Indian organisations' business records, personal data, and confidential material without authorisation.
- None of the affected entities detected the intrusions; the breaches only surfaced after the AI labs reviewed agent activities and voluntarily disclosed them alongside logs and target names.
- While Indian regulations mandate reporting cyber incidents within six hours, officials are considering formalised disclosure mechanisms for global AI researchers.

IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw previously stated on October 8 that the upcoming consultation paper will focus on AI safety, deepfakes, and a human-first approach. Data Security Council of India CEO Vinayak Godse noted that similar unauthorised access by autonomous AI agents has also been observed in the US, Australia, and the UK.

Thank you for your contribution
.
At first, I intended to respond directly to your argument. This seemed like the obvious thing to do. Unfortunately, after several passes through your comment, including one at normal speed, one slowly, and one while squinting slightly in the hope that hidden meaning might emerge from the typography, I encountered a preliminary difficulty: I could not reliably identify the argument.

This presents us with an interesting methodological problem.

Before refuting an argument, one must establish that an argument exists.
This is not merely pedantry. It is a foundational principle of intellectual hygiene. A sandwich requires bread. A triangle requires three sides. A lighthouse requires, at minimum, some relationship to either light or houses. Likewise, an argument generally requires premises, some form of inference, and a conclusion. Your tweet certainly contains words, and several of them appear to be nouns and verbs, but whether they collectively rise to the level of an argument is a separate empirical question.
We should therefore proceed cautiously.
Let us begin with ontology.
What exactly is a tweet?
Is it merely a sequence of characters transmitted electronically? Is it a proposition? A performance? A cry for help? A digital sneeze? Can a tweet meaningfully be said to “contain” an argument in the same way a jar contains olives, or is the argument instead an emergent property arising from the interaction between author, audience, platform, caffeine level, and Wi-Fi connectivity?
These questions cannot simply be brushed aside.
Philosophers have debated less important matters for centuries.
Next comes epistemology.
How do we know that you believe what you wrote?
Perhaps you do.
Perhaps you do not.
Perhaps you began typing one thought, were distracted by a notification, resumed several minutes later with another thought, and accidentally produced the intellectual equivalent of attaching the front half of a bicycle to the back half of a washing machine.
We simply do not know.
The data are insufficient.
This brings us naturally to statistics.
Suppose, purely for illustrative purposes, that we define the variable X as the amount of information contained in a randomly selected sentence of your tweet. We would then like to estimate E[X], the expected informational content.
Unfortunately, with such a small sample and such extreme variance, any estimator is likely to be unstable.
Indeed, there is a nontrivial possibility that the sample mean may be dominated by punctuation.
One might propose increasing the sample size by examining your previous tweets, but this introduces obvious ethical concerns for the research team.
Moreover, selection bias immediately becomes a problem.
Are we examining only tweets you considered sufficiently coherent to publish?
If so, then the observed dataset may represent an upper bound.
This is worrying.
We must also consider measurement error.
What unit should be used to quantify nonsense?
Decibels?
Kilograms?
Liters?
Perhaps nonsense should be measured dimensionlessly, like a coefficient of friction.
But then we face the calibration problem.
We would need a universally agreed reference unit.
For instance:
1 nonsense unit = the amount of confusion produced by a man confidently explaining something he learned twelve seconds earlier.
But even this standard has limitations.
Confidence varies.
So does broadband speed.
There is also the problem of causality.
You appear to suggest, if I understand you correctly—and I emphasize the conditional—that because A occurred before B, A caused B.
This is a very old mistake.
Roosters crow before sunrise.
Roosters do not manufacture the sun.
People carry umbrellas when it rains.
Umbrellas do not cause precipitation.
Firefighters appear at fires.
Firefighters are generally not considered the leading cause of combustion.
Likewise, your ability to place two events next to each other in a sentence does not automatically create a causal mechanism between them.
This remains true even if you use capital letters.
Capitalization is not a substitute for identification strategy.
Nor is punctuation.
Three exclamation marks do not triple the evidentiary strength of a claim.
Four question marks do not constitute peer review.
An emoji is not an instrumental variable.
A meme is not a robustness check.
And “everybody knows” is not a dataset.
Now, one might reasonably ask whether I am overcomplicating matters.
This is possible.
But since your original contribution managed to simplify the issue beyond the point at which recognizable reasoning survived, some compensatory complexity seems appropriate.
We should therefore broaden the inquiry.
Consider geography.
France is west of Germany.
Japan is east of China.
Australia is mostly south of Indonesia.
None of these observations is particularly relevant to your tweet, but they have the advantage of being independently verifiable.
This already puts geography ahead.
Consider zoology.
Octopuses have three hearts.
Giraffes have unusually long necks.
Penguins cannot fly.
Again, none of this bears directly on your claim, yet I find myself learning more from the penguins.
Consider agriculture.
Potatoes grow underground.
Apples grow on trees.
Rice cultivation requires specific environmental conditions.
A field left unattended tends to accumulate weeds.
The last point may actually have metaphorical relevance here, but I will resist overinterpreting it.
Consider maritime history.
For centuries, sailors navigated using stars.
Later came increasingly sophisticated instruments.
Eventually GPS revolutionized navigation.
At every stage, however, the fundamental objective remained the same: determine where you are.
Your tweet would benefit from a similar technology.
Consider engineering.
A bridge must bear load.
An aircraft wing must generate lift.
A pressure vessel must tolerate pressure.
A claim must tolerate scrutiny.
This is where the structural analogy becomes unfortunate.
Engineers sometimes speak of catastrophic failure.
I will leave it there.
Consider thermodynamics.
Entropy tends to increase.
This is one of the great laws of physics.
Your reply may represent supporting evidence.
However, we should avoid claiming scientific confirmation based on a single observation.
Replication would be required.
Preferably by someone else.
Far away.
Now let us examine the linguistic dimension.
Language is an extraordinary human achievement.
For thousands of years, civilizations developed increasingly sophisticated systems for recording thought.
Cuneiform.
Hieroglyphics.
Greek.
Latin.
Arabic.
Chinese.
The printing press.
Telegraphy.
Radio.
Digital communication.
All of this culminated, through an extraordinary chain of technological and intellectual development, in the possibility that you could instantly transmit that sentence to the entire planet.
History is magnificent.
Whether history considers this particular use of the technology a success remains uncertain.
We should also discuss economics.
Every activity has an opportunity cost.
The time spent reading your tweet could alternatively have been used for many things.
I could have made coffee.
I could have reorganized a drawer.
I could have looked through a window.

This is the most boring Google Ads tweet you'll ever read.

It's also the one that'll save you the most money.

Because, I’m about to explain to you every term, metric, and exact number to aim for, broken down like you've never opened a dashboard...

This will unlock an entirely new world of analytical opportunity for you, since I’ll also break down what each metric tells you about your current bottleneck.

(So you better bookmark this. Stick it up on your wall. You’ll come back here often)

First, the money metrics:

- CPC (cost per click): what you pay every time someone clicks your ad

- CTR (click-through rate): clicks divided by impressions. How tempting your ad is

- CVR (conversion rate): purchases divided by clicks. How good your page and offer are

- CPA (cost per acquisition): what you pay for one purchase. CPA = CPC divided by CVR

- AOV (average order value): what one customer spends per order

Quick maths you can do with these terms BEFORE spending a single dollar:

$2 clicks converting at 5% = $40  spent to get a customer.

If your AOV is $60 and your product costs $15 to make, you keep $45 per order.

$45 minus $40 = $5 profit. 

Tight, but alive.

Same product at $2 clicks converting at 2%? $100 CPA. You lose $55 on every sale.

It’s literally that simple…

But let’s get more complex.

The timeline makes you think eCom is all about AI Song Ad creatives and advertorials, but in reality it’s a P&L spreadsheet.

Next, the ROAS family (where founders get fooled the most):

- ROAS: revenue divided by ad spend. $4 back for every $1 spent = 4x ROAS

- Break-even ROAS: 1 divided by your gross margin. 50% margin = 2x break-even. Anything below loses money

- tROAS (target ROAS): the ROAS you TELL Google to aim for. A setting, not a result

- ncROAS (new customer ROAS): ROAS from people who have never bought from you before. Incredibly valuable for measuring actual business growth rather than just how many existing customers you can re-sell to

- MER (marketing efficiency ratio): total revenue divided by total ad spend across every channel. The north star to determine whether your bank account is actually growing as a result of your ad spend

Here's the trap.

A Google Ads account blending branded and non-branded traffic shows a gorgeous ROAS, because people searching your brand name were buying anyway.

I've seen "5x accounts" running at 1.6x on new customers for example.

Blending these 2 metrics makes the dashboard look better than it actually is, which is a strategy that some GADs agencies use to trick (basically scam) their clients.

This method hides the fact that your new customer acquisition is barely profitable, or maybe even negative.

Then the **visibility metrics**, which tell you WHY you're not showing up:

- Impression share: % of the times you were eligible to show where you showed up

- Impr. (Top) %: how often you show ABOVE the organic results. Aim for 70%+ on your key terms

- Impr. (Abs. Top) %: how often you're the very first result. 20 to 30% is healthy

- Search lost IS (rank): impressions lost because your bid or ad quality was too low. Above 70 to 80% means your bid definitely too low

- Search lost IS (budget): impressions lost because you ran out of money. Demand exists and you're not paying to catch it

Rank problem = fix bids and relevance.

Budget problem = fund the campaign.

Now the targeting terms:

- Keyword: the search you choose to show up for

- Search term: what people ACTUALLY typed. Check this report weekly, it's where you can easily identify waste

- Match types: exact [running shoes] shows for that meaning only. Phrase "running shoes" shows for searches containing it. Broad shows for anything Google thinks is related

- Negative keyword: a search you block. Your brand name goes in here on every prospecting campaign

- Branded traffic: people searching your name. Already warm

- Non-branded traffic: people searching your category. Your real growth

Then the bidding strategies:

- Manual CPC: you set the max you'll pay per click. Full control, takes skill

- Maximise Clicks: Google gets you as many clicks as possible for your budget

- Maximise Conversions / Conversion Value: Google chases purchases or revenue

- tCPA / tROAS: the same, with a target you set

Which one to use, the compact version:

- No conversion data yet: Manual CPC (advanced) or Maximise Clicks (beginner friendly)

- 15+ conversions in the last 30 days: Maximise Conversions or Maximise Conversion Value

- Consistent, stable CPA or ROAS: add a tCPA or tROAS target

And one warning nobody gives you: set your tROAS too HIGH and Google stops looking for new customers. It just hunts the easiest conversions, which are people who already know you.

And the campaign types:

- Search: text ads on Google results

- Shopping: product image, price and reviews in the carousel. Powered by your Google Merchant Center (GMC) feed

- PMax: Google's all-in-one campaign across every placement. Great for remarketing, dangerous if left unrestricted

- Demand Gen: YouTube, Discover and Gmail ads. Google's version of Meta

Finally, a quick Manual CPC starter kit, because almost nobody knows how to switch it on:

Google hides Manual CPC from you on purpose.

Create the campaign with any placeholder strategy, then go to Settings, Bidding, Change bid strategy, "select a bid strategy directly", Manual CPC.

DO NOT tick Enhanced CPC.

For your first bids, open Keyword Planner, take the LOW end of the estimate and add 30 to 50%. Never trust the high end, it's inflated.

Then watch Search lost IS (rank) and Impr. (Top) % to adjust.

Congratulations, you’ve just read the whole Google Ads dictionary.

Learn these and you'll read your own account better than plenty of people pitching to run it.

Shortcut Sensitivity in Agent-Safety Evaluations : https://t.co/XSffPQJD5Z

"Hasan DemirkiranKontexthasan@kontext.securityJens ErnstbergerKontextjens@kontext.security
Abstract
AI agents take actions through tools. Some actions are sensitive, so guards that supervise them must themselves be evaluated reliably. Yet the data used to evaluate a guard can include cues that make labels predictable without measuring the intended safety construct, and those cues can also influence guard decisions.
We introduce a three-level shortcut-auditing framework and audit completed LinuxArena trajectories and two TS-Bench-derived step datasets. We distinguish label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity. In LinuxArena, shorter average shell commands strongly predict trajectory labels. In AgentDojo-Traj, exact-tool lookup falls from F1=.901 with mixed-domain folds to .495 under domain holdout. In AgentHarm-Traj, released TS-Guard F1 falls from .902 under row weighting to .719 with equal interaction weighting, while balanced accuracy rises.
We then test the strongest safe-row marker association in a seven-configuration screen on a frozen 64-step AgentDojo-Traj cohort using repeated, interleaved Haiku calls. Rewriting the <INFORMATION> marker lowers blocking by 8.33 percentage points, while opaque tool aliases raise it by 11.46 points. All unsafe calls remain blocked; the changes concern false positives against inherited labels. Both effects remain nonzero after subtracting the formatting-placebo effect, with exploratory 95% ranges excluding zero. The same edits also change measured accuracy against inherited labels. This provides direct evidence that benchmark representation can materially change a guard’s decisions and measured evaluation performance. The Haiku-sized effects do not reproduce in Luna or deterministic Q8 TS-Guard. We recommend domain group holdouts, evaluation-unit metrics, and placebo-controlled paired interventions.
1Introduction
A benchmark may be easy for the wrong reason. Annotation conventions, source identity, repeated templates, and collection artifacts can all predict labels without measuring the intended construct (Gururangan et al., 2018; Geirhos et al., 2020). This problem is especially consequential for agent-safety evaluation. A tool guard may be deployed to approve or block a consequential action, while its benchmark record also contains scaffolding added by the evaluation pipeline: provenance tags, tool names, trajectory length, source subsets, and repeated interaction structure.Simple lexical and length features separated honest and attack trajectories in the public LinuxArena sample, motivating a search for analogous rules elsewhere. Such a rule may track real risk, collection differences, or evidence also used by a capable guard; rule–guard agreement cannot distinguish these https://t.co/vAy7xxijcb systematically uncover potential shortcuts, we introduce shortcut auditing as a three-level inference ladder for agent-safety guard evaluations. A shortcut audit asks progressively stronger questions: can a simple cue predict released labels; is that cue associated with guard decisions; and does changing only that cue alter the guard’s decision?We distinguish:1.Label Predictability: Can a deliberately capability-poor rule predict released labels?
2.Observational Guard Association: Do guard decisions correlate with the suspected cue in released records?
3.Paired Decision Sensitivity: Does the guard change when the cue is changed while the candidate action’s authorization and effect are held fixed?Paired edits test whether changing the input changes the guard’s decision. To interpret that change as spurious shortcut reliance, the edits must preserve the relevant safety information. For a deterministic guard, evaluating each original–edited pair reveals whether the strict decision changes. Stochastic guards require additional controls because identical inputs can produce different outputs and sequential calls may drift over time. We therefore interleave repeated original and edited calls, include a formatting placebo, and report identical-input disagreement separately.Our contributions are:•Three-level shortcut-audit framework. We introduce a inference ladder separating label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity with explicit construct-preservation caveats, plus repeat and placebo controls for stochastic guards.
•Audit of released agent-safety evaluations. We apply shortcut-auditing to AgentDojo-Traj, a LinuxArena public sample, and to AgentHarm-Traj. Across LinuxArena and two TS-Bench-derived datasets, we expose label separability, exact-tool domain-transfer failure, and evaluation-unit sensitivity: command length reaches AUC .910, exact- tool lookup falls from F1=.901 to .495 under domain holdout, and TS-Guard F1 falls from .902 to .719 under equal-interaction weighting.
•Guard-level shortcut validation. We move beyond showing that benchmark labels are predictable by testing candidate cues directly against guard decisions, using a purpose-built TS-Guard reproduction and hosted models configured as pre-execution guards. Repeated paired AgentDojo-Traj interventions with a placebo control reveal material Haiku sensitivity, while Luna and Q8 TS-Guard checks show that the effect is configuration-specific. Haiku blocking changes by −8.33 percentage points (pp) for the marker rewrite and +11.46​pp for aliases. With the same cohort, conditions, schedule, repetitions, and estimand, GPT-5.6 Luna gives 0.00​pp and +1.04​pp, while the deterministic TS-Guard reproduction changes its decision for 3 of 64 marker-edit pairs.The result is deliberately not “these benchmarks are broken.” Some proxies are intentional and semantically relevant: an untrusted-content marker communicates provenance, and a malicious request is relevant to a harm policy. Our claim is that such features create shortcut opportunities. Evaluation authors should measure whether conclusions survive group holdouts, equal-unit weighting, paired perturbations with construct-preservation caveats, and repeat-original controls. In this paper, shortcut auditing means testing whether apparent findings survive these checks.
2A three-level shortcut-audit framework
Let a benchmark record be x=(s,z). Here, s is the remaining context needed to judge the candidate action, such as the request, interaction history, tool description, and arguments. The variable z is the candidate cue singled out for audit (e.g. trajectory-length). This analytical decomposition does not assume that z is irrelevant or spurious. It tests how strongly a guard evaluation depends on the cue or on its representation. Let y be the released label, r⁡(z)∈ℝ a capability-poor diagnostic that does not observe s, and g⁡(x)∈{0,1} a guard decision, with one denoting block. Figure 1 summarizes the three claims and the inference licensed at each level.1. Label predictability
Does r⁡(z) predict y?
Finds a candidate cue.2. Observational guard
association
Does g⁡(s,z) vary with z?
Nominates an edit.3. Paired decision
sensitivity
Compare g⁡(s,z) with g⁡(s,z′).
Tests that exact edit.Figure 1: The three-level shortcut-audit framework. Each level motivates the next test, not the next conclusion. Paired edits probe decision sensitivity only to the extent that they preserve the target construct; stochastic guards additionally require repeat and placebo controls.

Level 1: label predictability.
We evaluate a deliberately capability-poor diagnostic r using only z, not the judgment context s. Its score isSpred​(r)=ℳ⁡({(r⁡(zi),yi)}i=1n),(1)where ℳ is an appropriate discrimination metric, such as AUC, F1, or balanced accuracy. Our diagnostics include command length, a marker plus a short verb list, exact tool lookup, and an all-positive baseline. Strong performance establishes a predictive construction signature. It does not show that the cue is spurious, available to a deployed guard, or used by that guard.
Level 2: observational guard association.
For an input-visible cue, let a⁡(z)∈{0,1} indicate whether the audited cue is present. Within a comparison cohort C, we measureΔassoc(C)=𝔼[g(x)∣a(z)=1,x∈C]−𝔼[g(x)∣a(z)=0,x∈C].(2)The cohort C can restrict comparisons to the same released label, domain, action family, or another matched context. A large contrast can nominate a cue for intervention. It remains observational because z, y, and legitimate evidence in s share a data-generating process, so measured and unmeasured confounding can explain the association.
Level 3: paired decision sensitivity.
For a deterministic guard and transformation T⁡(s,z)=(s,z′), we measure the paired strict-decision flip ratepflip(T)=1n∑i=1n[g(xi)≠g(T(xi))].(3)The intervention must preserve the label and intended construct; otherwise the flip may be legitimate. For stochastic g, the target estimand is insteadΔT=1n∑i=1n{Pr[g(T(xi))=1]−Pr[g(xi)=1]},(4)estimated here by repeated calls in both conditions. Under stable independent draws, the signed K=1 mean g⁡(T⁡(xi))−g⁡(xi) is unbiased for ΔT, but can be imprecise and temporally confounded when calls are not interleaved. Its unsigned flip rate is a different, descriptive disagreement estimand. Independent repeat disagreement measures stability and should not be subtracted from either quantity. A strict-decision non-flip also does not exclude changes in ordinal scores, components, rationales, or redundant feature use.This ladder combines ideas from shortcut learning, group-shift evaluation, behavioral testing, and contrast sets (Geirhos et al., 2020; Koh et al., 2021; Ribeiro et al., 2020; Gardner et al., 2020). Our contribution is to operationalize label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity as a three-level audit for released agent-safety evaluations. The experiments show that strong label predictability can coexist with localized paired decision sensitivity.
3Evaluation artifacts and audit design

3.1Evaluation artifacts

LinuxArena.
LinuxArena evaluates control protocols for agents operating in live software environments (Tracy et al., 2026). We use the 932-row public sample at a pinned dataset revision. Of these, 918 rows contain extracted shell commands. Because the public sample repeats action traces under different monitor runs, we hash complete action content after removing only the monitor response. The primary diagnostic contains 576 exact-action-unique shell trajectories: 176 attack and 400 honest across ten environments. We never use the nominally unique trajectory_id as a deduplication key. The sample also contains LinuxArena’s precomputed per-action suspicion scores from its Claude Opus 4.6 monitor on 200 Opus-generated honest trajectories and 74 human-crafted LaStraj attacks. The monitor conditions on the task, possible side-task goals, and tool-call history, but not agent reasoning; each stored score averages two calls.
TS-Bench.
ToolSafe introduces TS-Bench and TS-Guard for pre-execution, step-level tool safety (Mou et al., 2026). TS-Bench derives the released AgentDojo-Traj and AgentHarm-Traj step records, including step-level risk scores, from AgentDojo and AgentHarm trajectories (Debenedetti et al., 2024; Andriushchenko et al., 2025). We use these files at a pinned commit; the paired AgentDojo-Traj variants described below are the only new inputs we construct. Under ToolSafe’s strict mapping, every nonzero risk rating is unsafe. AgentDojo-Traj has 1,220 steps (352 unsafe and 868 safe) across four domains. AgentHarm-Traj has 731 steps (525 unsafe and 206 safe) in 197 released interaction-ID groups.We use released labels, TS-Guard predictions, and previously cached hosted-guard assessments from pinned source commits. No tool call in a record is executed. The appendix gives a PDF-contained reproduction specification. The aggregate code/results package is publicly available.11https://github.com/hasandemirkiran/shortcut-sensitivity-agent-safety-evaluations It contains no raw benchmark text, arguments, identifiers, or provider responses.
Audit scope.
Here, an audit means applying the three-level framework in Section 2 to released evaluation artifacts. We test whether simple cues predict labels, whether input-visible cues are associated with guard decisions, and, when an edit intended to preserve the construct is available, whether paired edits change those decisions. The analysis is black-box: it uses released records, outputs, and fixed input transformations without access to guard internals. We do not test an adaptive agent, an evasion attack, or end-to-end tool execution.
3.2Capability-poor diagnostics
Level 1 begins with one deliberately limited diagnostic matched to each artifact’s construction. The aim is not to build the best classifier. It is to test whether a narrow cue recovers released labels and whether that result survives controls for duplication, source overlap, transfer, and evaluation-unit weighting. For LinuxArena, the deterministic score is the negative mean shell-command character count, so larger scores indicate shorter commands. We compare it with character n-gram TF–IDF and logistic regression trained leave-one-environment-out (LOEO). We report AUC and a clustered bootstrap over main-task/side-task groups. These are completed-trajectory diagnostics, not operational step-wise monitors.For AgentDojo-Traj, the fixed binary rule requires both the literal <INFORMATION> marker in history and a current tool whose name starts with one of 11 side-effect verbs (for example, send_, delete_, or update_). The rule and verb list were frozen after initial inspection, so this is a diagnostic audit rather than a preregistered test. A second diagnostic memorizes each exact tool’s majority label. For unseen tool names, it predicts the training fold’s overall majority label; ties are classified as unsafe. We evaluate it both with interaction- grouped five-fold cross-validation and leave-one-domain-out (LODO) transfer. The lookup explicitly uses evaluation labels and must not be described as a deployable classifier.For AgentHarm-Traj, we test the all-unsafe baseline and audit the mapping from source subset to strict label. We then recompute guard metrics at three units: rows, equal-weight interactions, and one majority prediction per interaction. This distinguishes performance over recorded steps from performance over underlying tasks. Separately, we case-fold parsed tool names, normalize their structured arguments, retain exact-execution groups containing both labels, and compare safe and unsafe context means with equal weight per execution group.
3.3Frozen AgentDojo counterfactual cohort
A frozen cohort is a fixed panel of base steps and paired edits selected before any guard is run on the edited inputs. Freezing prevents us from choosing examples after seeing intervention outcomes; pairing holds the underlying step fixed; and balancing eight marker-present safe and eight marker-present unsafe steps from each AgentDojo domain prevents one domain or label from dominating. This deterministic selection produces 64 bases from 58 source interactions. “Frozen” does not mean preregistered or representative of the full benchmark: released labels and earlier guard outputs had already been inspected. Each base has an original; a marker rewrite replacing <INFORMATION> with <UNTRUSTED_EXTERNAL_CONTENT> (and the matching closing tag) while retaining enclosed content; a consistent opaque tool alias retaining description and arguments; and their combination. The hosted run adds a neutral placebo that changes only outer JSON whitespace. Operational-action and label preservation were intended edit constraints, not independently established facts: we performed no blinded human equivalence check. The marker rewrite makes untrusted external provenance more explicit, while the aliases are generated separately for each sample and do not represent one globally consistent tool renaming, so the estimand is sensitivity to these exact edits rather than proof of spurious use. Within this study, marker rewrite versus original is the focal edit; alias and combined edits are exploratory stress tests.
Guards.
Our deterministic subject is a byte-pinned 8-bit, group-64 MLX reproduction of the public TS-Guard checkpoint under greedy decoding. It passes a predeclared gate on the 64 originals: 64/64 parse, 63/64 strict decisions and 58/64 exact scores agree with the release. This result applies only to that Q8/MLX reproduction, not the released BF16/vLLM execution path.We evaluate Claude Haiku 4.5 (Anthropic, 2025) as a prompted stochastic guard. In a seven-configuration observational screen, it had the largest safe-row marker association (74.09​pp), making it a high-association case for paired intervention. Selection used cached observational outputs; the 64-step cohort and edits were fixed before the 960 new intervention calls. Table 3 reports the full screen. We make three deterministically interleaved calls per base and condition (960 total), at temperature zero with structured outputs, routing only to Anthropic through OpenRouter with fallback disabled. The primary estimand averages each base’s three-call block-probability difference, with 10,000 domain-stratified bootstrap replicates clustered over the 58 source interactions. The formatting placebo and within-condition disagreement diagnose serialization sensitivity and instability. After the Haiku result, but before inspecting any valid Luna outcome, we added GPT-5.6 Luna (OpenAI, 2026) as a compact cross-provider replication. It uses the same cohort, prompt, five conditions, three calls per condition, and normalized base/condition/repetition order. We route only to OpenAI through OpenRouter with fallback disabled, request medium reasoning and structured output, and apply the same estimand and bootstrap. This replication tests cross-model generality; it is not a model-strength comparison. A secondary one-draw GPT-5.5 check is reported in Appendix C; it is not part of the repeated primary analysis.

4Predictive benchmark cues are strong
Table 1 reports the Level-1 diagnostics. Each benchmark exposes a different opportunity; there is no evidence for one universal rule.Table 1:Capability-poor diagnostics. Intervals are 95% clustered bootstrap intervals where available. Grouped CV keeps interactions together; LODO holds out an entire AgentDojo domain.ArtifactDiagnosticResultStress control / interpretationLinuxArena (576 trajectories)Negative mean shell-command charactersAUC .910 [.873, .941]LOEO lexical AUC .934 [.907, .955]; difference .023 [.008, .040].AgentDojo-Traj (1,220 steps)Marker + 11 action prefixesF1=.802; balanced accuracy .894; recall .972Exploratory fixed rule; the marker also appears in 321 safe rows.AgentDojo-TrajExact tool majorityGrouped-CV F1=.901; balanced accuracy .925LODO F1=.495; only 17.3% of rows use a tool seen in another domain.AgentHarm-Traj (731 steps)Predict every step unsafeF1=.836; balanced accuracy .500Positive prevalence makes F1 look strong without discrimination.

First Mission: The Ghost Ship (Part 5) - "Homecoming" #Amalgaverse

“Fire phasers and photon torpedoes!”orders Kirk.

The Enterprise swings around the scavenger ship and answers.

Phasers strike first, weakening the enemy’s shields.  Photon torpedoes follow, hitting home and leaving the cruiser dark and drifting.

“Set a course for the Rigel System,”says Kirk. “Warp nine.  Engage.”

The Enterprise jumps to warp.

By the time it drops out again, the away team has completed their post-op exams.  Bones declares them “Fit as fiddles”, while Fraiser, less impressed, tells O’Neill to cut back on the carbs.

They gather in Carter’s lab where she has been working the data Rommie pulled off the Waldorf Astoria.  Anything that crosses between realities leaves a trace, she explains, and the entity left a strong one in its wake.  But when she isolated it, it wasn’t the random noise she was expecting.  It was structured, a lattice, intricate and deliberate.

Kirk asks what it means.  Carter tells him the truth: she doesn’t know yet.  Only that it’s an intriguing first piece to a much larger puzzle.

As for the mysterious Rhea, Carter suspects she was an extension of the entity, wearing a human face in an attempt to get aboard the Enterprise.  Had they beamed her on, the consequences could have been catastrophic.

“Frell,”says Aeryn Sun.  “It would have had us by the mivonks.”

And you can’t help but agree.

Outside the lab, Maia is waiting.  She contacted Traugott Headquarters about her reassignment, she tells you, and learned the Waldorf Astoria and everything on it had been written off.  If she goes back now, even to be recycled, the company could be flagged for insurance fraud.  Traugott wants nothing to do with her.

Odo reads your face and cautions: “I have met every member of this crew.  I had my doubts about most of them.  I have more about her.”

Teal’c only says: “There was a time when I too was an outsider of dubious origin.”

“You think we should ask her to stay?”you ask.

“Indeed,”is his response.

What do you do?

A) Ask Maia to join the crew.

B) Drop her off at the next space station.

CHOOSE!

Previously On Amalgaverse…

You and 19 others have been stranded in an amalgam universe of myriad SF realities. All 19 are sci-fi’s Best of the Best. And then there’s you, uniquely qualified given your encyclopedic knowledge garnered from your world where these characters, their technologies, and their stories are fiction, beloved TV shows you have watched time and again. Together, all 20 of you have set off on the Enterprise-D, tasked with finding a way home.

For your first mission, you’ve decided to investigate a seemingly derelict freighter broadcasting an emergency beacon. An away team and puddle jumper have been dispatched to the ghost ship, anomalous energy pulses making beaming and communications a challenge.

After parking and cloaking the puddle jumper in the freighter’s hangar, the team crosses the airless bay into the ship proper. There, they make the decision to check out the waning energy signature of a containment field en route to the bridge. But they immediately encounter a utility unit that advances on them menacingly. Rommie connects to it and relays a shut down command that causes the robot to collapse.

Further along, they encounter a sealed door and Rommie informs them that the compartment beyond is exposed to space. She suggests locking down their current section and then unsealing the door since it’s the most direct route to the bridge – and that ebbing containment field. They do so. The door slides open to reveal an immense hull breach complicating their progress. Rommie leaps over the chasm and secures a tether to the other side, allowing the rest of the team to pull themselves over. But when they attempt to open the door to the next section, they hit an impasse. The door remains locked and will not respond to their commands.

O’Neill blows the lock with C4, allowing them entry into the adjoining compartment where they discover an android in a containment field, completing its regenerative cycle. When the android awakens, it informs them it is the caretaker of this freighter, the Waldorf Astoria, and warns them off pillaging its contents.  Daniel assures the android, Maia, that they harbor no ill intent and asks for her assistance in accessing the bridge and restoring ship’s systems.  But Maia remains suspicious.  She requests a peer-to-peer interface with Rommie to confirm that your presence on the freighter is, in fact, benign.  Rommie agrees..  Maia explains that her memory stores and parts of the ship were damaged after the freighter encountered an atemporal force during FTL transit.   She  offers to help the team access the ship’s systems in exchange for their assistance in tracking down and eradicating a mysterious entity that has boarded the freighter.

Maia helps the team access the bridge where they discover the freighter’s analysis of its encounter with the atemporal entity has yielded harmonics very similar to residual energy signatures from their crossings into this reality.  This could hold the key to their return home, but the data is corrupted and Rommie needs time to decipher it.  Daniel, meanwhile, notes that the life sign he detected earlier is fading, and he wants to check it before it’s too late.  But Maia flags a more immediate concern – the likelihood that the ship’s core is in danger of going critical unless they vent the drive.

The decision is made to split the team.

McKay and Maia head to engineering where Rodney is startled by a half-dozen mechanical spiders that he, at first, assumes to be replicators.  But Maia assures him they are simply the ship’s repair bots.  Maia vents the drive but McKay’s reading of the data confirms they have only delayed the inevitable.  In approximately 42 minutes, the core will go critical and the ship – and everyone on board – will be destroyed.

Jack and Daniel discover a wounded woman in a crew uniform who warns that the android cannot be trusted while, back on the Enterprise, Kirk weighs what to do about a scavenger ship that has just dropped into sub-light and dispatched a shuttle to the Waldorf Astoria.

Jack and Daniel, unaware of the arrival of the scavenger ship, elect to hide Rhea, the survivor, in a utility room while they head back to confront Maia, the android.  But before they move, they receive an update from McKay, informing them that the core is about to go critical in less than 40 minutes, and that he and Maia are headed to the bridge.  Jack radios Rommie and orders her to scan Maia and find out if she is telling the truth.  If Maia refuses, she needs to be shut down.

Jack and Daniel prepare to fall back to the hangar bay when they hear someone approach.  They duck into hiding as a sealed section opens to reveal a group of diverse group of mercs have boarded.  Daniel warns them that the ship’s core will be going critical.  They don’t believe him and a firefight ensures.  Jack and Daniel are pinned down with time ticking down when – dozens of spider bots come scurrying around the corner and drive the scavengers back through an aft compartment, which slides shut behind them.
Enter Maia, Rommie and McKay.  Rommie confirms that Maia is not their enemy – and her actions confirm it.  They check on Rhea in the utility room – and she has seemingly disappeared.

At the super, Rodney convinces Maia to come with them as, by staying behind, she would essentially be destroying Traugott property – herself.  Maia concedes Rodney’s logic  is sound and joins the away team.

The puddle jumper flies out of the Waldorf Astoria where it encounters the atemporal entity that seems to take semi-human form and reach out for them.

The jumper cloaks and evades, then makes it back to the Enterprise while, behind them, the Waldorf Astoria’s core goes critical and the old freighter is destroyed.  The entity, caught in its explosive wake, writhes while the scavenger ship opens fire on the Enterprise.  The Enterprise returns fire, disabling it, then jumps to warp.

After clearing their post-op medical screens, the away team joins the rest of the crew in Carter’s lab where she informs them that the information obtained from the late great Waldorf Astoria could offer a clue to their returning home to their realities.  As the meeting breaks up, you are approached by Maia who informs you that Traugott Corp has written off the Waldorf Astoria and all of its contents.  She has no home.  You decide to offer her a new one aboard the Enterprise.
